Declare one more readonly property to return the actual values of blocks property.

Q: Getting "The operation has timed out" message on HttpWebRequest in Asp.Net Core A:

  1. What is the size of response data? If it is huge, you may get timeout exception.

  2. What is health of endpoint? Are you seeing any request time out issues when you try to ping from command prompt console?

  3. increase request timeout value:

request.TimeOut = 3600; // milli second value

Q: The type initializer for 'Gdip' threw an exception in kubernetes pods with C#.net core A:

Is there any way to fix this issue from C# side . Not interested to add/modify build scripts

No. System.Drawing.Common has platform dependencies. They are always there on Windows, but must be installed on Linux.

NOTE that on Ubuntu (and other Linuxes) you may need to install some native dependencies as System.Drawing sits on top of native libraries

sudo apt install libc6-dev
sudo apt install libgdiplus

https://www.hanselman.com/blog/how-do-you-use-systemdrawing-in-net-core

Q: optional prerequisites in gnu make A:

Optional dependencies in makefile rules are generally a bad idea. In this particular case of yours, the builder/user is deprived the choice of building a.out without a.supplement even when a.suppsrc exists.

Despite this shortcoming, you can still do it with a trick of making a do-nothing target for a.suppsrc:

a.suppsrc:
  true

Then do what you want to do with shell script conditionals:

a.supplement: a.suppsrc
  if [ -f a.suppsrc ]; then \
    $(SUPPBUILD) -o $@ -i $< \
  fi

a.out: a.in a.supplement
  if [ -f a.supplement ]; then \
    $(BUILDER) -o $@ -i @< supplement:a.supplement \
  else \
    $(BUILDER) -o $@ -i @< \
  fi

That's it. The do-nothing target for a.suppsrc is to prevent Make from complaining that there is no rule to make a.suppsrc when the file doesn't exist.

Q: Why is git hanging when a push appears nearly done? A:

Git's not hanging, it's waiting for the OS to tell it everything actually made it to the storage medium.

Seriously: a write being accepted takes microseconds. A write makeing it to storage media takes milliseconds. That's a factor of a thousand, and it gets worse: a large-ish chunk of that delay is per separate operation, so if the OS can batch up a hundred or writes that's a hundred or so milliseconds saved in getting them all done.

Now: there's a glitch I've seen in some hardware combinations on Windows, I no longer recall the exact circumstances, but the solution was to turn off the Windows write caching on the ssd. device manager, pick your drive, google says properties, policies, turn off write caching and that sounds about right. This worked for me on a previous rig, its cheap SSD was dropping to a ridiculous 10MB/s write rate after a few seconds of steady (and fast) writes and this brought the floor up to a more tolerable 150 or so.

Q: Least‑privilege permissions for Azure AI Foundry agents deployed to Microsoft Teams (avoid Azure AI User for end users) A:

Is Azure AI User the correct role for end users, or is it intended only for developers/operators?

It is most certainly not the correct role for end users. Like you mentioned, it gives more permissions to the user which enables them access to AI Foundry Projects and agents.

We tried creating a custom role with just read permissions but unfortunately that did not work either.

Microsoft is aware of this issue and I believe they are coming up with a new role similar to Azure AI User role but with a key difference - you should be able to apply that role at the agent level (currently the lowest level at which the roles can be applied is at the Project level).

If you have Prompt Agents, then the solution is to publish that agent. Once an agent is published, you can give Azure AI User role to that user.
